config.title: Build a health check endpoint

intro.title: Build a health check endpoint
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple health check endpoint for a Node.js server, which is a common API route that reports whether your application is running correctly. You will learn how to create a basic HTTP server using Node.js's built-in `http` module and define a specific route that responds to requests. The core programming concepts involve handling HTTP requests, sending appropriate status codes, and returning JSON-formatted data. By the end, you'll have a working endpoint that returns a status message, helping you understand the fundamentals of server setup and API response handling in Node.js.
intro.usecase: Health check endpoints are a foundational pattern in production software, used by monitoring dashboards and orchestration tools to verify service availability. For example, a cloud operations dashboard might poll this endpoint to display a 'live' or 'degraded' status for your API, while Kubernetes uses it to automatically restart unhealthy containers. As a developer, implementing this endpoint is a critical step for building reliable, observable systems that can be managed at scale.

objectives: Construct a basic Express server with a designated port
Implement a GET route for the health check endpoint
Configure the endpoint to return a JSON response with status information
Initialize a response object containing server status and timestamp
Integrate the health check endpoint into the main application flow
Manipulate the response to include dynamic uptime or version data
Apply middleware to handle errors for the health check route

steps.title: Import Express framework
steps.instruction: Import the Express module using require() and assign it to a variable named 'express'.
steps.hint: Use the require() function to import the 'express' package and store it in a variable.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing a module in Node.js
const fs = require('fs');
steps.expectedOutcome: The Express module is imported and ready to use.
successCriteria: The 'express' variable is declared and assigned the imported Express module.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported Express using require().
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using require() and assigning it to a variable named 'express'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import the Express module using require('express').

steps.title: Create Express application instance
steps.instruction: Create a constant named 'app' and assign it the value of calling the imported express() function.
steps.hint: Use the imported 'express' function to initialize your application instance.
steps.analogousExample:
// Creating an application instance
const app = express();
steps.expectedOutcome: An Express application instance is created and stored in a constant named 'app'.
successCriteria: A constant named 'app' is declared and assigned the result of calling express().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling the express() function to create the instance and storing it in a constant named 'app'.
steps.feedbackWrong: create an Express application instance by calling the imported express() function and storing it in a constant named 'app'.

steps.title: Define the health check endpoint route
steps.instruction: Define a GET route at '/health' using app.get() that sends a JSON response with status: 'ok'.
steps.hint: Use app.get() with the route path '/health' and a callback function that sends a JSON response using res.json().
steps.expectedOutcome: A GET route at '/health' is defined that returns a JSON response with status: 'ok'.
successCriteria: The route uses app.get() with '/health' and sends a JSON response with status: 'ok'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using app.get() with '/health' and sending a JSON response with status: 'ok'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The route isn't defined correctly. Use app.get() to create a GET route at '/health' that sends a JSON response with status: 'ok'.

steps.title: Create the health check response handler
steps.instruction: Inside the route definition, add a callback function that takes request (req) and response (res) parameters and sends a JSON response with a status message.
steps.hint: The callback function should look like: (req, res) => { ... } or function(req, res) { ... }. Use res.json() to send a JSON response.
steps.expectedOutcome: The route now has a handler function that can process requests and send responses.
successCriteria: The /health route has a callback function with req and res parameters that uses res.json() to send a JSON response.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function takes both req and res parameters and uses res.json() to send a response.
steps.feedbackWrong: The route handler isn't quite right. It needs to be a function that takes req and res parameters and sends a JSON response.

steps.title: Set response status code
steps.instruction: Inside the health check route handler, use the response object's status() method to set the HTTP status code to 200.
steps.hint: The status() method is called on the 'res' parameter and takes a number as its argument.
steps.analogousExample:
// Setting a success status code
res.status(200);
steps.expectedOutcome: The health check endpoint will respond with a 200 OK status code.
successCriteria: The route handler includes res.status(200) to set the status code.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're calling status(200) on the response object inside the route handler.
steps.feedbackWrong: The status code isn't set correctly. Use res.status(200) inside the route handler function.

steps.title: Send JSON response with health status
steps.instruction: Inside the route handler, use res.json() to send a JSON object with a status property set to 'healthy'.
steps.hint: Call res.json() with an object like { status: 'healthy' }.
steps.expectedOutcome: The /health endpoint will respond with a JSON object containing the health status.
successCriteria: The route handler uses res.json() to send a JSON object with a status property set to 'healthy'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using res.json() with an object like { status: 'healthy' }.
steps.feedbackWrong: The response should be sent using res.json() with a JSON object containing the status.

steps.title: Add server timestamp to response
steps.instruction: Inside the health check route handler, add a 'timestamp' field to the JSON response object with the current server time using Date.now().
steps.hint: The Date.now() method returns the current timestamp in milliseconds. Add it as a property in your response JSON object.
steps.expectedOutcome: The health check endpoint will return a JSON response containing both the health status and a server timestamp.
successCriteria: The JSON response includes a 'timestamp' field with the current server time value from Date.now().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the timestamp field is properly included in the JSON response object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The timestamp field is missing or not properly implemented. Check that you're adding it to the response JSON object.

steps.title: Start the server on a specific port
steps.instruction: Add the app.listen() method call at the end of your file to start the server on port 3000.
steps.hint: Use app.listen(3000) to make your Express application listen for incoming HTTP requests on port 3000.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your Express application will be ready to handle HTTP requests on port 3000.
successCriteria: The app.listen(3000) method is called to start the server.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Your server is now configured to listen on port 3000.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling app.listen() with port 3000 as the first argument.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server isn't started yet. Use app.listen(3000) to make your application listen for requests.

steps.title: Add console log for server startup
steps.instruction: Add a callback function to the app.listen() call that logs a message to the console when the server starts successfully.
steps.hint: The callback function should be the second argument to app.listen() and use console.log() to display a message.
steps.expectedOutcome: The server will log a startup message to the console when it begins listening for requests.
successCriteria: app.listen() has a callback function that logs a message using console.log()
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added a callback function to app.listen() that uses console.log() to display a message.
steps.feedbackWrong: The server startup message isn't properly configured. Add a callback function to app.listen() that logs a message to the console.

steps.title: Export the Express application
steps.instruction: Export the Express application instance using module.exports so it can be imported and tested elsewhere.
steps.hint: Add module.exports = app; at the end of your file to make the app instance available for external use.
steps.analogousExample:
// Exporting a module in Node.js
module.exports = myModule;
steps.expectedOutcome: The Express application instance is exported and ready for testing or integration with other modules.
successCriteria: The app instance is exported using module.exports.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're exporting the app instance using module.exports.
steps.feedbackWrong: The app instance is not exported correctly. Use module.exports to export the app variable.
